title: Judaism: hear
hookLine: the central declaration: hear, O Israel, the Lord is one (Deuteronomy 6:4)

lines: SIX HEBREW WORDS, TWICE A DAY.
cards: Six Hebrew words. Observant Jews say them twice a day, morning and night, often with a hand over the eyes. They're whispered to children at bedtime.
They're written on a tiny scroll inside a case on the doorframe of Jewish homes. And Jewish tradition hopes they will be among a person's last words. The striking part is the very first word.
It isn't believe, or pray, or obey. It's listen. Today's word: Shema.

teach.b: The words come from Deuteronomy, chapter six, verse four, where Moses speaks to the people before they enter the land.
In the Jewish Publication Society's 1917 translation: "Hear, O Israel: the LORD our God, the LORD is one." In Hebrew, it begins Shema Yisrael.

teach.h: SHEMA: HEAR, HEED, TAKE TO HEART.
teach.b: Shema means hear, but it's a rich word: listen, pay attention, understand, take it to heart, even obey. It's hearing that changes what you do.

And notice who's addressed: not one person alone, but Israel, the whole people. Then the next verse: "And thou shalt love the LORD thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy might."

The passage goes on: these words should be on your heart, taught to your children, spoken when you sit at home and walk on the road, when you lie down and when you rise up, bound on your hand and written on your doorposts.
Observant Jews do exactly that. The Shema is said in the morning and evening prayers.
It's written inside the mezuzah on the doorpost and inside tefillin, the small leather boxes some Jews bind on the arm and head for weekday morning prayer.
The custom is to cover the eyes while saying it, shutting out everything else to listen.
A guest's note: when Jews read the divine name, written in English as LORD, they don't pronounce it, but say Adonai, my Lord, instead.
The Talmud tells of Rabbi Akiva, put to death by the Romans, dying with the Shema's last word, one, on his lips. The center of Jewish faith begins with an open ear.

how: Observant Jews recite the Shema in the morning and evening prayers and at bedtime, often covering their eyes; its words are written in the mezuzah on the doorpost and in tefillin.

o: pray: ask God for help at the start of each day
believe: accept God's existence without question
hear: listen, pay attention, take it to heart

games.q: you're a guest at a Jewish prayer service. everyone covers their eyes and says six words together. what do you do?
o: sit quietly and listen with them.
games.why: the Shema is a moment of listening. a guest can simply be still and hear it; questions can wait until afterward.

practice: If you like, cover your eyes with your hand, as is the custom for the Shema, and just hear: the nearest sound, then something farther away, the hum of the room, your own breath.
Don't name them or judge them; let hearing be the whole practice.

wordCard.voice: Shema. Hebrew for hear, listen, take to heart: the first word of Judaism's central declaration, said morning and night. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: hear. Fully, to take it to heart, not just waiting for your turn. Day two hundred forty-six, done.
